items.title: Not every landlord should switch to Airbnb
items.script: Not every landlord should put their property on Airbnb. Ask three things: is there genuine local demand, do the lease and rules allow it, and do you want the work involved? If one answer is no, a traditional let may be better. Airbnb is a business model, not a magic upgrade. Save this before switching.
items.visualElements: Close-up talking head outside a rental. On-screen title: ‘Not every landlord should switch to Airbnb’. Cut to three numbered cards: Demand, Rules, Operations. End on a calm exterior shot.

items.title: The Airbnb income number that misleads landlords
items.script: A high nightly rate can be the most misleading number in Airbnb. £180 a night is not automatically better than £120. You must account for occupancy, cleaning, utilities, maintenance, fees and your time. Compare the net outcome after the property has actually been run, not one impressive screenshot.
items.visualElements: Talking head with title: ‘£180 a night can still be a bad deal’. Overlay a simple calculator: rate minus occupancy, cleaning, utilities and fees. Use B-roll of cleaning and a guest-ready room.

items.title: Can a normal two-bed flat work on Airbnb?
items.script: You do not need a penthouse for Airbnb to work. A normal two-bed can be great, but it needs real demand, a useful layout, clear building rules and something that suits the guest. The answer is in the demand and the detail, not whether it looks like a five-star hotel.
items.visualElements: Film in a tidy two-bed flat. Title: ‘Can a normal 2-bed work on Airbnb?’ Show bedroom, desk, parking or transport, and building exterior. Overlay: Demand, Layout, Rules, Guest fit.

items.title: What happens when a guest locks themselves out at 11pm
items.script: This is what people forget when they say, ‘I’ll just manage it myself.’ A guest locks themselves out at 11pm. You need to reply quickly, restore access, know who can help if the lock fails, and still protect the guest experience. Without a system, one late-night problem becomes a bad review.
items.visualElements: Start at a front door in low light, holding a phone. Title: ‘Guest locked out at 11pm’. Show a blurred mock message, keypad and three overlays: Reply, Restore access, Escalate.

items.title: How good operators reduce the risk of guest damage
items.script: The biggest Airbnb fear is usually damage. No property is zero-risk, but good operators do not rely on hope. They use clear rules, sensible guest screening, documented checks, high cleaning standards and fast action. The point is not eliminating every problem. It is catching problems early.
items.visualElements: Talking head in a living room. Title: ‘Guests will trash my property?’ Cut to house rules, a cleaner checklist, inspection photos and a room check. Finish on a clean wide property shot.

items.title: Why a full Airbnb calendar can still underperform
items.script: A fully booked Airbnb calendar can be a warning sign. If every night is taken at too cheap a rate, you may be leaving money on the table. The goal is the right mix of price, stay length, guest type and workload. A busy calendar looks great. A commercially sensible one is better.
items.visualElements: Open on a generic full calendar on a phone. Title: ‘Fully booked can be a warning sign’. Use a simple graphic: Cheap and full versus right price and profitable. Show linen turnover B-roll.

items.title: The hidden cost of managing Airbnb yourself
items.script: Most landlords only calculate what they might save by self-managing. They do not calculate the work: messages, cleaners, pricing, check-ins, maintenance, reviews and holiday emergencies. You can self-manage, but price your time honestly. If it needs you available all day, it is not passive income. It is another job.
items.visualElements: Phil at a desk. Title: ‘The hidden cost of self-managing’. Rapid B-roll of phone notifications, cleaning rota, laptop calendar, keys and a maintenance call. End by closing the laptop.

items.title: Traditional let or Airbnb? Start with this
items.script: Do not choose between a traditional let and Airbnb based on rent alone. Start with your goals, the rules, local demand, running costs and how involved you want to be. For some landlords, a long-term let is right. For others, short stays fit better. The property should decide the strategy, not a TikTok video.
items.visualElements: Split screen labelled Traditional let and Airbnb, with Phil in the middle. Add five text overlays: Goals, Rules, Demand, Costs, Time. Cut between exterior and guest-ready interior.

items.title: The first 48 hours after a guest checks out
items.script: A great Airbnb stay is often won before the next guest arrives. We are not just changing sheets. We inspect, spot maintenance issues, restock essentials, check the clean and make sure the next guest walks into what they expected. Turnover is the system that protects the review, property and next booking.
items.visualElements: Open a property door after checkout. Use B-roll of inspection checklist, making beds, restocking coffee, checking light bulbs and final room photos. Title: ‘What happens after checkout?’

items.title: Why ‘just put it on Airbnb’ is bad advice
items.script: ‘Just put it on Airbnb’ is bad advice. Uploading photos is easy. The real work is market research, pricing, preparing the property, handling guests, cleaning, maintenance and standards. A listing is not a business model. The operation behind it is what makes it work.
items.visualElements: Start tapping Publish on a mock listing. Title: ‘Uploading is the easy bit’. Fast cuts: pricing calendar, photographer, linen, guest message and maintenance kit. End talking head: ‘The operation is the business.’

items.title: What great Airbnb photos actually do
items.script: Great Airbnb photos are not decoration. They set expectations: layout, light, workspace, sleep, parking and the real experience. When photos tell the truth well, you attract the right guests and avoid disappointed ones. The best photos do not make a tiny room look huge. They make the right guest feel confident.
items.visualElements: Phone with a listing photo grid. Title: ‘Photos are not decoration’. Show photographer framing rooms, then finished photos full-screen. B-roll of desk, bed, parking and local view.

items.title: The question to ask before furnishing an Airbnb
items.script: Before you buy one cushion, decide who the guest is. Contractors, families, couples and business travellers need different things. The guest should drive beds, workspace, storage, dining and the welcome pack. Furnishing for your own taste is expensive. Furnishing for demand is a strategy.
items.visualElements: Film in a property or furniture shop. Title: ‘Before you buy furniture…’. Show four overlays: Contractor, Family, Couple, Business traveller. Cut to workspace, twin beds, storage and dining table.

items.title: Why Airbnb reviews are an operating system
items.script: A bad Airbnb review is rarely just a bad review. It is usually a clue. Maybe check-in was confusing, the clean was not good enough or a small maintenance issue was missed. Good operators ask what part of the system allowed that experience, then fix it before the next guest.
items.visualElements: Talking head with a blurred one-star review behind him. Title: ‘A bad review is a system failure’. Overlay: Check-in, Clean, Maintenance, Expectations. Show a checklist being updated.

items.title: What Lougher & Co actually manages
items.script: When a landlord asks what Airbnb management includes, here is the short version. We help assess the property, set it up properly, manage pricing, handle guests, coordinate cleaning and maintenance, and protect the small details that drive reviews. You own the property. We run the operation, so it does not take over your life.
items.visualElements: Talk to camera in a polished property. Title: ‘What we actually manage’. Use a five-stage timeline with B-roll: Assess, Set up, Price, Guests, Operations. Finish on the property exterior with subtle branding.

items.title: The seasonality mistake landlords make
items.script: The same Airbnb strategy does not work every month. Demand changes with events, holidays, business travel and the market. If you use the same price and expectations all year, you are managing on autopilot. Good short-stay management means planning ahead, not panicking when the calendar changes. Airbnb is not a fixed monthly number.
items.visualElements: Calendar changing from summer to winter. Title: ‘Airbnb is not the same every month’. Show Phil reviewing a blurred pricing calendar, seasonal local B-roll and overlays: Plan, Price, Adapt.

items.title: Why local knowledge beats generic Airbnb advice
items.script: Generic Airbnb advice can be dangerously confident. What works in one city can be wrong two hours away. Demand might come from hospitals, contractors, events, universities or tourism. The right property, guest and price depend on what is actually happening around it. Before copying someone else’s model, understand your own postcode.
items.visualElements: Film outside a recognisable local landmark or using a local map. Title: ‘Your postcode changes the strategy’. Add map pins for transport, hospital, city centre, venue and business park.

items.title: Three signs your rental may need a strategy review
items.script: Your rental may be worth a strategy review if it is in an area with short-stay demand, has features guests value like parking or a workspace, and you have flexibility in how it is let and managed. That does not mean Airbnb is automatically right. It means you should review the numbers rather than assume the current setup is best.
items.visualElements: Title: ‘3 signs your rental needs a review’. Phil counts three points on fingers. Use B-roll of parking, workspace, extra bedroom and transport. End text: ‘Review numbers, not assumptions.’

items.title: More bookings does not always mean more money
items.script: More bookings does not always mean more money. Ten one-night stays can mean more cleaning, more check-ins, more issues and more workload than two well-priced longer stays. The target is not simply full occupancy. It is the right mix of revenue, guest fit and work for that property.
items.visualElements: Whiteboard or phone note: ‘10 one-night stays’ versus ‘2 longer stays’. Title: ‘More bookings ≠ more money’. Show rapid turnover B-roll, then a calm guest-ready room. Keep a small footer: ‘It depends on the property.’

items.title: What I would check before switching a long-term let to Airbnb
items.script: If this was my long-term rental, I would check five things before moving it to Airbnb: permissions and lease, genuine demand, honest numbers after every cost, whether the layout works for the guest, and who runs it when something goes wrong. If you cannot answer all five, do not rush the switch.
items.visualElements: Walking property tour. Title: ‘Check these 5 things first’. Match numbered overlays with lease paperwork, map, calculator, bedroom layout, phone and keys. End at the front door with a save prompt.

items.title: The landlord freedom test
items.script: Here is the landlord freedom test. If your Airbnb needs you answering messages all day, coordinating cleaners, changing prices at night and fixing problems on holiday, you have built another job. Good management is not just tasks being done. It is a system, accountability and a good guest experience when you are not thinking about the property.
items.visualElements: Close talking head. Title: ‘Freedom or another job?’ Cut between notifications, cleaning calendar and suitcase. Then switch to calm B-roll of a guest-ready property and operations checklist. End with Phil walking away from the property.
